Learning Objectives
Review the classification of pediatric musculoskeletal infections and the definition of complex
pediatric musculoskeletal infections.
Identify the most common causative organisms of pediatric musculoskeletal infections.
Explain the acute phase response and the manner in which certain bacteria use virulence
factors to manipulate and evade the immune system.
Perform an appropriate evaluation of pediatric patients in whom musculoskeletal infections is
suspected.
Specify the appropriate management for complex pediatric musculoskeletal infections.

Classification
Pediatric musculoskeletal infection (MSKI) is classified based on tissue type (superficial
abscess, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, deep abscess/pyomyositis, complex infection) and/or
severity (inflammation, local infection, and disseminated infection).
Complex MSKI is an infection involving more than one tissue type, multifocal infection, and/or
infection with evidence of systemic involvement.
Disseminated infection is associated with more severe disease and poorer hospital outcomes.

Classification
Pediatric MSKI can be classified based on the type of tissue infected and also by the
severity of infection1 (Resource 1). The classification of MSKI based on tissue type
includes superficial abscess, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, deep abscess/pyomyositis,
and complex infection2 (Table 1). Using this classification system, complex MSKI may be
defined as infection in more than one tissue type, including any combination of bone,
muscle, and joint infection (eg, ischial osteomyelitis with surrounding pyomyositis and
abscess of the obturator internus muscle)2 (Resource 2).

MSKI also can be classified based on the severity of illness. This classification system is
useful because it can predict outcomes (Table 2). Three categories exist: inflammation,
local infection, and disseminated infection. Inflammation includes patients with a
negative local tissue culture, a negative blood culture, and no criteria met for local or
disseminated infection.2 Local infection includes patients with imaging studies diagnostic
for osteomyelitis or pyomyositis in one anatomic site, a positive local culture and/or
fluid/tissue consistent with infection, a positive blood culture, and no criteria met for
disseminated infection. Disseminated infection includes patients with two or more
anatomic sites affected with imaging studies diagnostic for osteomyelitis or pyomyositis,
a positive local culture and/or fluid/tissue consistent with infection, two or more positive
blood cultures, and thromboembolic disease. Patients with disseminated infection have
longer hospital length of stays, undergo a greater number of surgical procedures,
undergo a greater number of positive blood cultures, undergo a longer duration of
antibiotic therapy, have longer intensive care unit (ICU) length of stays, have a greater
number of days with fever, and undergo a greater number of imaging studies.2
Therefore, complex pediatric MSKI can be defined as infection involving more than one
tissue type (bone, muscle, and/or joint), multifocal infection affecting two or more
anatomic sites, and/or infection with evidence of systemic involvement (two or more
positive blood cultures, thromboembolic disease, or systemic inflammatory response
syndrome [SIRS]/sepsis). Examples of complex pediatric MSKIs are shown in Figure 1.2

Epidemiology
Rule out MSKI consults represent almost 10% of all orthopaedic consultations.
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism of pediatric MSKI. In patients
younger than 5 years, Kingella kingae is an important pathogen.

Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL) toxin is a virulence factor commonly found in community-
acquired Methicillin-resistant S aureus (MRSA) that leads to increased severity of disease and
poorer outcomes.
Traditional culture methods are less effective for detecting K kingae. A polymerase chain
reaction (PCR) test should be used to evaluate for K kingae infection in children younger than 5
years.

Epidemiology
At large academic, pediatric tertiary care centers, MSKI-related consultations (including
rule out MSKI and confirmed infections) account for a mean of 3,000 consults per year,
or 9.3% of all orthopaedic consultations.3 Complex MSKI may be difficult to diagnose
because the patient presentation is similar to that of isolated septic arthritis, isolated
osteomyelitis, or isolated deep abscess/pyomyositis. Surgeons must recognize complex
MSKI because these types of infections are associated with poorer outcomes.
The exact incidence of complex MSKI is difficult to determine because of regional and
epidemiologic variation. Institutional differences in the work up of MSKI and the
availability of advanced imaging studies likely contribute to an underestimation of
complex MSKI. Mignemi et al4 reported on 53 pediatric patients who presented to the
emergency room with a rule out septic hip. Of those patients, 47% had a complex
infection about the hip joint. The prevalence of isolated septic arthritis and isolated
pyomyositis was 15% and 32%, respectively.
The most common causative organism in pediatric MSKI is S aureus. Other causative
organisms to consider include Group B Streptococcus in children younger than 12
months and K kingae and Streptococcus pneumoniae in children younger than 5 years.
MRSA results from mecA gene transfer to S aureus, resulting in beta-lactam resistance.
The incidence of MRSA MSKI has increased over the past several decades. MRSA is
associated with greater severity of infection because of the presence of virulence factors,
including PVL.5 PVL is a cytokine that leads to cell and tissue necrosis and is associated
with more severe disease, including a higher incidence of complex infection, multifocal

7/22

infection, prolonged fever, thromboembolic disease, sepsis, and multiorgan failure.6
Patients with MRSA infections also have longer hospital length of stays, more time spent
in the ICU, and an increased need for surgical débridement.7 PVL is more commonly
found in community-acquired MRSA and less often found in hospital-acquired MRSA. The
methicillin resistance does not lead to severe disease; instead, the presence of these
virulence factors lead to severe disease. Methicillin sensitive S aureus also can express
PVL and can cause severe disease on par with that of MRSA.7
The incidence of K kingae MSKI recently has increased, likely because of improved
detection methods. K kingae is a gram-negative coccobacillus that mainly occurs in
children 4 years and younger. It is the causative organism in 50% of septic arthritis cases
in children younger than 2 years. K kingae has a low virulence and typically causes only
mild elevation of inflammatory markers. PCR from local tissue is the best method to
detect K kingae, and the test should be performed in all children younger than 5 years in
whom MSKI is suspected. PCR substantially improves the rate of K kingae detection
compared with joint fluid culture.8
Basic Science
Acute Phase Response
The acute phase response (APR) is the body’s reaction to tissue injury via coagulation,
inflammation, and tissue regeneration/repair.
Through the expression of virulence factors, bacteria are able to hijack the APR and evade the
body’s immune system to cause severe, disseminated infection.

Acute Phase Response
The APR is a systemic reaction to tissue injury that is mediated by the liver by the
modulation of more than 1,000 genes.9 The APR results in the production of acute-phase
reactants that allows humans to recover from injury via coagulation, inflammation, and
tissue regeneration. An inadequate response leads to hemorrhage, infection, and

AAOS | Complex Pediatric Musculoskeletal Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004061
8/22

impaired tissue regeneration, whereas an overexuberant or prolonged response may
lead to coagulopathy, venous thromboembolism, systemic inflammatory response
syndrome (SIRS), multiorgan failure, and death. Bacterial proliferation and virulence
factor expression during MSKI damages affected tissue. The tissue injury persists until it
is resolved by the body’s immune system, antibiotic agents, and/or surgical
débridement. Therefore, MSKI can be thought of as continuously activating the body’s
APR until management occurs. Patients with complex MSKI have a high infection burden
and, therefore, greater activation of the APR. This translates to an increased risk of
systemic complications, such as venous thromboembolism, sepsis/SIRS, multiorgan
failure, and even death9,10 (Resource 3).
Bacteria express virulence factors that allow them to colonize and disseminate within
the human body by hijacking the APR11 (Figure 2). The coagulation phase of the APR is
the body’s initial defense mechanism against bacterial infection. Bacteria are trapped
within fibrin/platelet clots followed by recruitment of leukocytes to the site of infection
as part of the body’s immune response. Coagulase, a virulence factor expressed by S
aureus, activates the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin, which then catalyzes the
cleavage of fibrinogen to fibrin. Von Willebrand factor-binding protein plays a similar
role, allowing the bacteria to form a double-layer fibrin-dependent barrier (abscess),
effectively shielding it from the body’s immune response. After bacterial proliferation
within the abscess reaches a critical mass, S aureus staphylokinase production leads to
fibrin degradation, abscess rupture, and dissemination of infection.9,10

Figure 2 Illustrations show the manner in which Staphylococcus aureus hijacks the
fibrinolytic system to disseminate. A, As the S aureus colony density increases, the
bacteria begin expressing staphylokinase, which converts plasminogen to its active
zymogen and plasmin (1). Plasmin breaks down the protective capsule, enabling S aureus
to escape its abscess (2). S aureus colonizes distant sites via hematogenous
dissemination (3). B,S aureus hematogenous dissemination via staphylokinase
expression and fibrin capsule degradation. Staphylokinase expression is upregulated
during the stationary phase of S aureus colony growth. (Reproduced with permission
from Benvenuti M, An T, Amaro E, et al: Double-edged sword: Musculoskeletal infection
provoked acute phase response in children. Orthop Clin North Am 2017;48[2]:181-189.)
Staphylococcus pyogenes uses a different method to invade and disseminate within the
human body. Streptokinase, a virulence factor expressed by S pyogenes, binds to and
activates plasmin, leading to the rapid degradation of fibrin and fibrinogen. This allows
for dissemination because the body is unable to form a network of fibrin clots to trap the
bacteria. An example of this is necrotizing fasciitis, a type of complex MSKI frequently
caused by S pyogenes. Necrotizing fasciitis is a highly invasive infection that disseminates
rapidly throughout the body because of its ability to bypass the coagulation phase of the
APR.9,10,12
Virulence factor expression varies not only between species, but also among bacteria of
a single species. This leads to tremendous variation in activation of the APR, and

therefore severity of illness, in patients with MSKI. Tissue damage caused by MSKI
generates measurable increases in acute phase reactants within the body. Therefore,
markers of inflammation and coagulation (C-reactive protein [CRP] level, fibrinogen,
platelets) are excellent indicators of disease severity. Elevated CRP level is a risk factor
for thromboembolic disease.13-15
Evaluation
Patient History/Physical Examination
The goal is to make a quick and efficient diagnosis of pediatric MSKI so the appropriate
treatment can begin as soon as possible after patient presentation.
A thorough physical examination of the patient is essential to locating all areas of potential
infection.
Children with complex MSKI should be examined for signs of systemic involvement.

Patient History/Physical Examination
Thorough diagnosis and management of pediatric MSKI is a challenge because MSKI
represents a spectrum of disease that is not always isolated to one tissue type or
anatomic location. Although septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and pyomyositis/abscess can
and do occur in isolation, these types of MSKI frequently occur in combination. Failure to
recognize complex MSKIs that involve more than one tissue type/anatomic location may
lead to delayed management, prolonged hospitalization, and an increased risk of
complications. The ideal clinical workup for patients in whom MSKI is suspected includes
a physical examination, laboratory tests, and appropriate imaging studies to make a
quick and efficient diagnosis.
Children with complex MSKI present with a combination of fever; elevated inflammatory
markers (CRP level, erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR], and white blood cell count
[WBC]); refusal to bear weight; joint irritability with decreased range of motion; and
localized tenderness, warmth, swelling, and erythema at the site of infection. Joint
irritability is most common if septic arthritis is a component of the infection. Kocher

criteria (ESR >40 mm/hr, fever >101.3°F [38.5°C], WBC >12,000 cells/mm3, inability to
bear weight) can be applied to children in whom concern for a septic hip exists; however,
Kocher criteria cannot distinguish isolated hip arthritis from complex periarticular hip
infection.4
The evaluation of a child in whom complex MSKI is suspected should begin with a careful
patient history and physical examination. In younger children, including infants and
toddlers, assessing the exact location of potential infection may be difficult. In addition,
more than one site of infection may be present. Therefore, surgeons must assess all
children presenting with possible MSKI for any and all sites of possible infection.
All patients with complex MSKI should be carefully evaluated for systemic complications,
which are driven by an exuberant APR. Systemic complications include sepsis/SIRS,
coagulopathy, thromboembolic disease, and multiorgan failure. Children with signs of
systemic involvement should be considered for admission to the ICU while awaiting
treatment so they can be more closely monitored. In children who are severely ill with
very elevated inflammatory markers, antibiotic treatment should not be delayed until
the patient is able to go to the operating room. Initiation of early antibiotic treatment
may help to lessen the APR and does not decrease the rate of positive local tissue
cultures.16,17 Thromboembolic complications of MSKI include septic pulmonary emboli
(SPE) and/or deep vein thrombosis (DVT). If a patient is severely ill or fails to respond to
initial surgical débridement/antibiotic treatment, a chest radiography and/or chest CT
should be considered to assess for SPE and Doppler ultrasonography should be
considered to evaluate for DVT.
Copley et al5 developed a severity of illness score for patients with MSKI based on initial
CRP level, CRP level at 48 and 96 hours, number of febrile days, band percentage of the
WBC differential, ICU admission, and presence of disseminated/multifocal disease. This
scoring system serves as an objective measurement of disease severity and may help
guide management in terms of need for surgery, ICU admission, and so forth.18
Laboratory Evaluation

Inflammatory markers are essential to the workup of pediatric MSKI.

Laboratory Evaluation
Laboratory evaluation should include WBC with differential, CRP level, and ESR.
Inflammatory markers are higher in children with complex MSKI than in those with
isolated infection (septic arthritis or osteomyelitis). All children in whom concern for
MSKI exists should have blood cultures sent on presentation. Blood culture can provide
valuable information regarding the causative pathogen because many children with
MSKI have positive blood cultures but negative local tissue cultures. Platelet count also
may be a useful laboratory study in evaluating children for MSKI. Initially, platelet counts
increase because the APR attempts to wall off infection via the formation of
fibrin/platelet clots. Prolonged activation of the APR leads to consumption of coagulation
factors, including platelets. Therefore, lower platelet counts on presentation are
associated with more severe disease, thromboembolic disease, and poorer outcomes.19
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs should be obtained for every child in whom suspicion for MSKI exists.
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for the diagnosis MSKI in children.

Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs should be obtained for every child in whom concern for MSKI exists.
Plain radiographs are inexpensive and readily available and can be used to rule out
trauma or other bone pathology, such as tumor. In patients with acute infection, a plain
radiograph almost always appears normal; however, subtle joint space widening may be
observed if a large joint effusion is present. Soft-tissue swelling appreciated on plain
radiographs may be indicative of underlying infection. Radiographic bony changes from
osteomyelitis typically are not observed until 7 to 14 days after the onset of infection and
until 30% to 40% loss of bone from the infection occurs. Long-term sequelae of MSKI,
including involucrum/sequestrum, osteonecrosis, growth arrest, angular deformity, and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Complex Pediatric Musculoskeletal Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004061
13/22

joint destruction, also may be appreciated on plain radiographs. Ultrasonography also is
a readily available and cost-effective imaging modality. Although ultrasonography can be
used to demonstrate the presence of a joint effusion, it has limited ability to identify
contiguous periarticular bone or muscle infection. CT has a limited role in acute MSKI.
Although CT can detect large soft-tissue abscesses, it is not as effective for evaluating
smaller areas of infection or early infection in bone. In patients undergoing workup for
SPE, CT is the preferred imaging modality. CT also aids in evaluating for chronic
osteomyelitis or late sequelae of MSKI, including osteonecrosis, growth arrest, and joint
destruction.9
Given the increased recognition of complex MSKI that involves more than one anatomic
location or tissue type, MRI has become the preferred imaging modality for MSKI.
Because MRI can image soft tissue and bone, it can detect sites of contiguous infection,
such as pericapsular pyomyositis adjacent to proximal femur osteomyelitis. In a study of
patients presenting to the emergency room with concern for septic hip arthritis, the
prevalence of pericapsular pyomyositis was found to be twice as common as isolated
septic hip arthritis.4 In a similar study, 48% of patients presenting to the emergency
room with concern for septic hip arthritis had osteomyelitis, and 25% of patients had a
combination of septic arthritis and adjacent osteomyelitis.20 The incidence of isolated
osteomyelitis was as common as isolated septic arthritis. In a study by Rosenfeld et al,21
age older than 3.6 years, CRP level higher than 13.8 mg/dL, duration of symptoms
greater than 3 days, platelet count less than 314 × 103 cells/μL, and absolute neutrophil
count higher than 8.6 × 103 cells/μL were found to be predictive of adjacent infection in
children in whom concern for septic arthritis existed, especially if three of the five
variables were present (Resource 4). Therefore, MRI is recommended in children in
whom concern for MSKI exists because of its superior ability to detected complex MSKI,
which is becoming an increasingly recognized condition. In addition to diagnosis, MRI
can provide substantial assistance in surgical planning by identifying all foci of infection
that must be addressed.
Unfortunately, MRI is not readily available at all institutions and it often necessitates
sedation in young children. To improve MRI use, many institutions have developed a
rapid MRI protocol for pediatric patients in whom concern for MSKI exists, with MRI
obtained without sedation in less than 30 minutes. Some institutions have created

programs that include an MSKI MRI slot that allows the patient to be taken from the MRI
scanner directly to the operating room during the same anesthetic event. Ojeaga et al22
demonstrated that using a multidisciplinary approach, which includes anesthesia,
radiology, and orthopaedic surgery, may lead to a decrease in scan duration, fewer
sequences per scan, a higher rate of procedures under the same anesthesia event as the
MRI, and an overall shorter hospital length of stay for the patient. MRI with contrast is
not necessary in most patients with acute MSKI but may increase the detection of very
small abscesses.
Management
Surgical Management
All areas of infection with a drainable fluid collection should be adequately débrided.

Surgical Management
Children with complex MSKI should be treated in a manner similar to those with isolated
infection. In children with substantially elevated CRP levels, surgeons should consider
initiating antibiotic agents as soon as blood cultures have been obtained. Surgical
débridement of any and all areas of drainable fluid collection is recommended.
Performing MRI before surgical management may aid in the recognition of areas of
involvement so that all sources of infection that are amenable to débridement are
adequately addressed. Local tissue cultures should be obtained and sent for analysis to
help determine the causative organisms. Anaerobic, fungal, and acid-fast bacillus
cultures should not be routinely performed in children in whom suspicion of acute
hematogenous MSKI exists unless the patient has a history of immunocompromise,
penetrating trauma, or failed primary treatment.17 If available, a PCR test for K kingae
should be performed in children 5 years or younger because K kingae is a common cause
of MSKI in children in this age group.
Antibiotic Therapy

If clinically indicated because of the severity of illness, antibiotic therapy may begin
immediately after blood cultures are obtained.
Antibiotic therapy should be tailored to the most common causative organisms and to local
epidemiology in terms of virulence factors/antibiotic resistance.

Antibiotic Therapy
Patients with acute MSKI should be started on empiric antibiotic therapy to cover the
most common organisms based on their demographics. Because of geographic variation
of causative organisms, antibiotic therapy should be targeted to local epidemiology. For
example, an increasing trend toward clindamycin resistance is observed in patients with
MRSA infections in some parts of the country, whereas clindamycin is the preferred
antibiotic agent for MRSA in other geographic locations.
Ample evidence suggests that initiating antibiotic agents before obtaining local tissue
cultures does not lower the likelihood of a positive culture. Therefore, antibiotic agents
may be initiated as soon as blood cultures are obtained in any patient in whom MSKI is
suspected. This is especially important in patients with very elevated inflammatory
markers, who appear ill, or have hemodynamically instability because antibiotic therapy
often is the first step in halting the body’s exuberant/prolonged APR.16,17,23
Response to management should be closely monitored. CRP level and ESR should be
assessed in a serial fashion to evaluate for improvement. An appropriate response to
management includes resolution of fever, decreasing inflammatory markers, and
improvement in clinical examination. If patients do not respond to initial treatment,
repeat surgical débridement or a change in antibiotic therapy may be required.
Inflammatory markers that rise or stay the same for 24 to 48 hours after surgical
débridement is not uncommon; however, a downward trend in response to
management should be observed after that. Repeat MRI after surgical débridement is
not suggested because images are difficult to interpret in the postoperative setting;
however, if a new area of concern exists or surgical management was not performed,
repeat MRI is appropriate if the patient does not improve.

Complications
DVT/SPE
DVT is a frequent complication of pediatric MSKI, and the risk of DVT is increased with more
severe infection.

DVT/SPE
DVT is rare in children but frequently is associated with MSKI and often is located
adjacent to the site of infection. Several studies have noted that children with
osteomyelitis and DVT are more likely to have elevated inflammatory markers, longer
hospital length of stay, increased number of surgical procedures, and more frequent ICU
admissions.14,24-28 Specifically, 82% of children with osteomyelitis and DVT have
bacteremia, versus 38% of children without DVT; 63% of children with DVT require ICU
admission versus 6% of children without DVT; and the mean number of surgical
procedures was two in children with DVT versus less than one in children without DVT.
All children with DVT in a child study had a CRP level higher than 8 mg/dL. Children with
osteomyelitis and DVT are more likely to have complex MSKI (multifocal or contiguous
septic arthritis) than those without DVT (54% versus 19%). Ligon et al15 reported that the
rate of MRSA infection was is higher in children with osteomyelitis and DVT (89%) than in
those without (21%) (Resource 5), which is similar to that reported in other studies.14 In
addition to DVT, SPE also are observed in children with severe MSKI. The incidence of
SPE has been reported to be as high as 64%.14 Based on these findings, children with
MSKI should undergo a workup for DVT via ultrasonography if any of the following are
present: CRP level higher than 8 mg/dL on presentation, WBC band percentage greater
than 1.5%, bacteremia, or suspicion/confirmation of SPE on chest radiographs or CT
scans. Similarly, a study found that every 2 mg/dL increase in peak CRP level was
associated with a 29% increased risk of thrombosis.13 Any child who fails to improve
despite adequate surgical débridement and antibiotic therapy also should undergo
ultrasonography to evaluate for DVT and chest radiography to assess for SPE. If SPE is
suspected, the diagnosis is best made via chest CT. Children with thromboembolic

Long-Term Outcomes
Outcomes in complex pediatric MSKI are favorable if diagnosis and management are
performed quickly and efficiently.

Long-Term Outcomes
The overall prognosis for complex pediatric MSKI is favorable if the diagnosis is made
quickly and appropriate management is initiated. Patients with complex MSKI are at risk
for chronic osteomyelitis with sequestrum/involucrum, pathologic fracture, growth
arrest leading to limb-length discrepancy and/or angular deformity, and joint
destruction. In patients with complex MSKI affecting a substantial portion of bone or
those who require extensive bony débridement to manage the infection, a period of
non–weight bearing is recommended to avoid pathologic fracture. Little evidence
suggests which patients are most at risk and how long weight-bearing restrictions should
be used.
